noteBlocks.lede: Heat blue copper(II) sulfate and it turns white; add water and the blue comes back. Some reactions run both ways, the conditions decide the direction, and in a sealed container the two directions settle into a balance.

noteBlocks.md: Most reactions you have met run one way and stop. A few run both ways: the products can turn back into the reactants, and the conditions decide which way the reaction goes. Blue crystals that turn white when heated, and blue again when water is added, are the example to keep in mind.

noteBlocks.caption: A single arrow claims one way only; the reversible sign claims both ways at once.

noteBlocks.md: A **reversible reaction** is one in which the **products can change back into the reactants**. Heat blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate and it loses its water; add the water back and the blue crystals re-form. Burning magnesium is not reversible: no change of conditions turns magnesium oxide back into magnesium and oxygen. A reversible reaction is written with the sign $\ce{<=>}$, never a single arrow.

noteBlocks.title: Why the sign earns its own mark
noteBlocks.md: A one-way arrow says the reaction finishes and the reactants are gone. The reversible sign says something different: both reactions are happening, so reactants and products are present together. The symbol is the claim, which is why schemes give it its own mark.

noteBlocks.stem: Nitrogen dioxide, $\ce{NO2}$, forms dinitrogen tetroxide, $\ce{N2O4}$, in a reversible reaction. (a) Give a balanced symbol equation, with the reversible sign. [4] (b) What is meant by a reversible reaction? [1]

steps.working: Left-hand side: $\ce{NO2}$, the reactant.
steps.decision: Formulae first. The reactant goes on the left; its formula is given, so copy it exactly.

steps.working: Right-hand side: $\ce{N2O4}$, the product.
steps.decision: The product goes on the right, as a separate mark from the left-hand side.

steps.working: Balance: $\ce{2NO2}$, because one $\ce{N2O4}$ holds 2 N atoms and 4 O atoms.
steps.decision: Count each element on both sides; a big number in front multiplies the whole formula.
The reversible sign is a mark of its own: a single arrow claims the reaction goes one way only.

steps.working: (b) The product, dinitrogen tetroxide, can change back into the reactant, nitrogen dioxide.
steps.decision: Name products and reactants. 'It can be reversed' or 'it returns to its original state' earns nothing.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which symbol is used in the equation for a reversible reaction?
noteBlocks.explain: The reversible sign, two half-arrows pointing opposite ways, claims both directions at once, as step 4 of See it wrote it. A single arrow claims the reaction runs one way and finishes, and an equals sign belongs in maths, not in a chemical equation.

optionNotes.why: The arrow of an ordinary equation claims the reaction runs one way and finishes; a reversible reaction does not.
An equals sign belongs in a maths equation; a chemical equation needs an arrow or the reversible sign.

twin.prompt: In the equation for a reversible reaction, what does the ⇌ sign tell you?
options: both the forward and the reverse reaction can happen
the reaction has stopped
the reaction gives out heat
twin.answer: both the forward and the reverse reaction can happen
twin.explain: The two half-arrows point both ways: the reactants can form the products and the products can re-form the reactants, as step 4 of See it showed.

optionNotes.option: the reaction has stopped
optionNotes.why: Nothing in the sign says a reaction has stopped; it says both directions are possible.

optionNotes.option: the reaction gives out heat
optionNotes.why: The sign says nothing about heat; an energy change is shown by a temperature change or a profile.

noteBlocks.prompt: A student writes that a reversible reaction is 'a reaction that can be reversed'. Why does this not earn the mark?
options: it never says the products can change back into the reactants
it should say the reaction returns to its original state
it should give an example that uses a catalyst
noteBlocks.answer: it never says the products can change back into the reactants
noteBlocks.explain: The mark is for the products changing back into the reactants, named as step 5 of See it wrote it. 'Can be reversed' only repeats the word being defined, and 'original state' names neither the products nor the reactants.

optionNotes.option: it should say the reaction returns to its original state
optionNotes.why: 'Original state' names neither the products nor the reactants, and the 2025 report says it lost the mark.

optionNotes.option: it should give an example that uses a catalyst
optionNotes.why: A catalyst has nothing to do with whether a reaction is reversible; the definition is about products and reactants.

twin.prompt: A student writes that a reversible reaction 'goes back to its original state'. Why does this lose the mark?
options: it names neither the products nor the reactants
it should say the reaction can be reversed
it forgets to mention the reversible sign
twin.answer: it names neither the products nor the reactants
twin.explain: The scheme wants the products changing back into the reactants, both named, as step 5 of See it wrote it; 'original state' names neither.

optionNotes.option: it should say the reaction can be reversed
optionNotes.why: 'Can be reversed' only repeats the word; it earns nothing either.

optionNotes.option: it forgets to mention the reversible sign
optionNotes.why: The sign belongs in an equation; a definition in words needs the products and reactants named.

noteBlocks.text: 2. The copper(II) sulfate test, both ways

noteBlocks.md: **Heat** blue **hydrated copper(II) sulfate** and the water bonded in its crystals is driven off as steam, leaving **white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate**. **Add water** to the white powder and it turns **blue** again, and the tube **gets hot**. In words: hydrated copper(II) sulfate $\ce{<=>}$ anhydrous copper(II) sulfate + water.

noteBlocks.title: Colours the scheme accepts
noteBlocks.md: Give both colours whenever you describe a change: **white to blue** on adding water, **blue to white** on heating. One colour on its own earns nothing, and 'clear' or 'colourless' is not white.

noteBlocks.stem: Adding water to white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate makes the tube hot. (a) Is the reaction with water exothermic or endothermic? [1] (b) What must happen to heat when the blue crystals are heated to turn them white again? [1]

steps.working: (a) Exothermic: heat is given out, so the tube gets hot.
steps.decision: The warm tube is the evidence; heat given out is what exothermic means.

steps.working: (b) Heat must be taken in: the reverse reaction is endothermic.
steps.decision: A reversible reaction that gives out heat one way takes the same amount in the other way.

steps.working: So the blue crystals must be heated to turn white: the flame supplies the heat that direction takes in.
steps.decision: The heating is not only to speed things up; the reverse direction needs that energy.

noteBlocks.title: GCSE Chemistry Revision "Reversible Reactions"
noteBlocks.why: The blue-to-white change run both ways, beside our own steps.

noteBlocks.prompt: Ammonium chloride splits into ammonia and hydrogen chloride when heated, and the two gases join to form ammonium chloride again as they cool. The splitting takes heat in. What does the joining do?
options: it gives out heat
it takes heat in as well
it has no energy change
noteBlocks.explain: A reversible reaction that takes heat in one way gives the same heat out the other way. Step 2 of See it showed it for copper(II) sulfate: adding water gave heat out, so heating the crystals took it in.

optionNotes.option: it takes heat in as well
optionNotes.why: Both directions cannot take heat in: whatever one direction takes in, the other gives back out.

optionNotes.option: it has no energy change
optionNotes.why: The splitting takes heat in, so the reverse cannot be zero: it gives the same amount out.

twin.prompt: Nitrogen dioxide forms dinitrogen tetroxide and gives out heat. What happens to heat when dinitrogen tetroxide turns back into nitrogen dioxide?
options: heat is taken in
heat is given out as well
no heat is involved
twin.explain: Heat out one way means the same heat in the other way, as step 2 of See it showed for copper(II) sulfate.

optionNotes.option: heat is given out as well
optionNotes.why: If both directions gave heat out, energy would appear from nowhere; one gives out, the other takes in.

optionNotes.option: no heat is involved
optionNotes.why: The forward reaction gives out heat, so the reverse cannot be zero: it takes that heat back in.

noteBlocks.md: Start a reversible reaction in a **sealed** vessel. The forward reaction begins fast and slows as its reactants are used up; the reverse reaction begins at zero and speeds up as the products build. When the two **rates become equal**, the reaction is at **dynamic equilibrium**: each substance is made as fast as it is used up, so the **amounts of reactants and products stay constant**.

noteBlocks.title: Why it is called dynamic
noteBlocks.md: Nothing has stopped: both reactions are still running, at the same rate as each other. It only looks still from outside, because nothing changes overall. Equal rates, not equal amounts: the amounts themselves are usually quite different from each other.

noteBlocks.stem: The graph shows the rates of the forward and reverse reactions for a reaction in a sealed flask. (a) At what time is equilibrium reached? [1] (b) What is true of the two rates from then on? [1] (c) Explain why the amounts of reactants and products then stay constant. [1]

noteBlocks.prompt: On a rate–time graph for a reaction in a sealed flask, the forward and reverse rates meet at 25 s and then run together. What happens to the amounts of reactants and products after 25 s?
options: they stay constant
they become equal to each other
they both fall to zero
noteBlocks.explain: From the moment the rates are equal, each substance is made as fast as it is used up, so its amount stays the same: step 3 of See it. The amounts are not equal to each other, and nothing falls to zero because both reactions keep running.

optionNotes.option: they become equal to each other
optionNotes.why: Equal rates, not equal amounts: the amounts stop changing at whatever values they have reached.

optionNotes.option: they both fall to zero
optionNotes.why: Both reactions keep running at equilibrium, so neither the reactants nor the products run out.

twin.prompt: On the same kind of graph, the two rates meet at 80 s. Which statement is true at 40 s?
options: the forward rate is still greater than the reverse rate
the amounts of reactants and products are constant
the two rates are equal
twin.answer: the forward rate is still greater than the reverse rate
twin.explain: Before the curves meet, the forward rate is still falling towards the reverse rate, which is still rising, as the graph in See it showed before its meeting point.

optionNotes.option: the amounts of reactants and products are constant
optionNotes.why: The amounts only stop changing once the rates are equal, which is later, at the meeting point.

optionNotes.option: the two rates are equal
optionNotes.why: They are only equal from the meeting point on; before it the forward rate is the larger.

noteBlocks.md: Dynamic equilibrium needs a **closed system**: nothing can get in or out. Heat limestone in an open tube and the carbon dioxide escapes into the room, so it can never react with the calcium oxide to re-form calcium carbonate. The reverse reaction never keeps pace and the rates never become equal. In a sealed tube the carbon dioxide stays, so both reactions can run.

noteBlocks.stem: Calcium carbonate is heated in a sealed tube and in an open tube: $\ce{CaCO3 <=> CaO + CO2}$. Explain why only the sealed tube can reach a dynamic equilibrium. [2]

steps.working: In the open tube the carbon dioxide escapes, so it cannot react with the calcium oxide.
steps.decision: Name what escapes: a gas leaving is what stops the reverse reaction.

steps.working: So the reverse reaction cannot keep pace and the rates never become equal; in the sealed tube nothing escapes, so they can.
steps.decision: Finish with the rates: equilibrium is defined by them, so the explanation has to reach them.

noteBlocks.prompt: A reversible reaction that makes a gas is carried out in an open beaker. Why can it never reach a dynamic equilibrium?
options: the gas escapes, so the reverse reaction cannot keep pace
the temperature keeps changing
the forward reaction stops at once
noteBlocks.answer: the gas escapes, so the reverse reaction cannot keep pace
noteBlocks.explain: A product that escapes cannot react back, so the reverse rate never catches up with the forward rate, as step 1 of See it said of the carbon dioxide from limestone. Sealing the vessel keeps every substance in.

optionNotes.option: the temperature keeps changing
optionNotes.why: A closed system is about substances getting in or out, not about heat.

optionNotes.option: the forward reaction stops at once
optionNotes.why: The forward reaction keeps going; it is the reverse reaction that cannot keep pace once a product escapes.

twin.prompt: The same kind of reaction is carried out in a stoppered flask instead. Why can it now reach a dynamic equilibrium?
options: the gas cannot escape, so the reverse reaction can keep pace
the stopper keeps the heat in
the stopper stops the forward reaction
twin.answer: the gas cannot escape, so the reverse reaction can keep pace
twin.explain: With nothing escaping, the product stays and reacts back until the two rates are equal, as step 2 of See it said of the sealed tube.

optionNotes.option: the stopper keeps the heat in
optionNotes.why: Keeping heat in is not the reason: a closed system stops substances escaping.

optionNotes.option: the stopper stops the forward reaction
optionNotes.why: Both reactions keep running in a stoppered flask; that is what makes the equilibrium dynamic.

noteBlocks.md: Changing the **temperature**, the **pressure** or the **concentration** of a reactant or product changes the **direction** of a reversible reaction, and so changes the amounts of reactants and products present. Learn all three as a set: most candidates name temperature and stop (2025 report).

noteBlocks.title: Where this specification stops
noteBlocks.md: Other boards ask which way the reaction shifts, using Le Chatelier's principle. CCEA's Double Award stops at 'the direction changes': you are never asked to predict which way.

noteBlocks.stem: Brown nitrogen dioxide and colourless dinitrogen tetroxide are at equilibrium in a sealed syringe: $\ce{2NO2 <=> N2O4}$. The plunger is pushed in and the colour of the gas changes. (a) Name the condition that was changed. [1] (b) What does the colour change show? [1]

steps.working: (a) The pressure.
steps.decision: Pushing the plunger squeezes the same gas into a smaller space, which raises the pressure.

steps.working: (b) The amounts of nitrogen dioxide and dinitrogen tetroxide have changed: the direction of the reaction changed.
steps.decision: A colour change means a change in amounts. CCEA asks only that the direction changes, not which way.

noteBlocks.prompt: A reversible reaction is at dynamic equilibrium in a sealed flask. More of one reactant is added. What happens?
options: the direction changes, so the amounts of reactants and products change
nothing changes, because it is at equilibrium
both reactions stop
noteBlocks.answer: the direction changes, so the amounts of reactants and products change
noteBlocks.explain: Concentration is one of the three conditions, with temperature and pressure: altering it changes the direction, and so the amounts, as the colour in step 2 of See it showed. An equilibrium is not frozen; it responds to a change.

optionNotes.option: nothing changes, because it is at equilibrium
optionNotes.why: Equilibrium only means the rates are equal now; change a condition and the direction changes.

optionNotes.option: both reactions stop
optionNotes.why: Neither reaction stops; the balance between them shifts until the rates are equal again.

twin.prompt: A reversible reaction at dynamic equilibrium in a sealed flask is cooled. Which statement is right?
options: the amounts change, because the direction of the reaction changes
cooling cannot change a reaction at equilibrium
only the forward reaction slows, so the amounts stay the same
twin.answer: the amounts change, because the direction of the reaction changes
twin.explain: Temperature is one of the three conditions that change the direction, and a changed direction changes the amounts, as step 2 of See it showed for pressure.

optionNotes.option: cooling cannot change a reaction at equilibrium
optionNotes.why: Temperature is one of the three conditions that change the direction of a reversible reaction.

optionNotes.option: only the forward reaction slows, so the amounts stay the same
optionNotes.why: If the rates stop being equal the amounts must change; they stay constant only while the rates match.

noteBlocks.md:
**Tick two statements** (2021, 2022). A list of six or eight; two are true: the rates are equal, and the amounts stay constant. The traps are amounts equal, both reactions stopped, and half reactants, half products.
**Complete the sentence** (2025). Two gaps, one for the rates and one for the amounts: rates first, amounts second.

**Why constant?** (2024). 'Explain why the amounts remain constant' wants the rates: the forward and reverse rates are equal. Saying the concentration does not change only repeats the question.
**The sign and the states** (2024, 2026). An equilibrium equation needs $\ce{<=>}$, and state symbols when they are asked for.
**Temperature** (2025). Changing it changes the direction, and so the amounts.

noteBlocks.stem: The reaction $\ce{2NO2 <=> N2O4}$ has reached dynamic equilibrium in a sealed syringe. Explain why the amount of dinitrogen tetroxide stays constant. [1]

steps.working: The forward reaction makes dinitrogen tetroxide and the reverse reaction uses it up, both all the time.
steps.decision: Start from what is still happening: both reactions run.

steps.working: The forward and reverse reactions run at the same rate, so it is made as fast as it is used up.
steps.decision: The mark is for the equal rates. 'Its concentration does not change' only repeats the question (2024 report).

noteBlocks.prompt: A reaction is at dynamic equilibrium in a sealed flask. The forward reaction makes 0.6 g of product every second. How many grams of product does the reverse reaction use up every second?
noteBlocks.explain: Equal rates means the product is used up exactly as fast as it is made: 0.6 g every second. That is why its amount stays constant, step 2 of See it.

twin.prompt: At dynamic equilibrium in a sealed flask, the forward reaction uses up 1.5 g of reactant every second. How many grams of reactant does the reverse reaction re-form every second?
twin.explain: The rates are equal, so the reactant is re-formed as fast as it is used up: 1.5 g every second, as in step 2 of See it.

noteBlocks.md:
Say what reversible means: the products can change back into the reactants.
Write the equation with ⇌, and give the copper(II) sulfate test both ways.
Define dynamic equilibrium: in a closed system, rates equal, amounts constant.
Explain why the system must be closed: nothing escapes, so both reactions run.
Name the three conditions that change the direction: temperature, pressure, concentration.

Equilibrium is in every C2 paper: a few marks at Foundation (the sign, a condition, what reversible means) and 4 to 8 marks at Higher, as Q2, Q4, Q7 or Q8 since 2019. The first mark is often the reversible sign; the definition is rates first, amounts second. Stuck? Write what is equal, then what is constant.

items.stem: In a chemical equation, what does the arrow mean?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 §1.5 — reading an equation; you are not expected to have met equilibrium yet

options.text: turns into
options.feedback: Reactants turn into products. This lesson changes that arrow into one with two heads, and the change of symbol is the whole idea.

options.text: is equal to
options.feedback: An equation balances, but the arrow is not an equals sign: it shows a direction, which is exactly what this topic is about.

options.text: is mixed with
options.feedback: Mixing is what the plus sign shows. The arrow shows the change.

items.stem: What is the rate of a reaction?

options.text: how much change happens in each second
options.feedback: An amount divided by a time. This lesson compares two rates in the same container.

options.text: how much product is made altogether
options.feedback: That is the total, with no time in it. A rate always has a time underneath.

options.text: how long the reaction takes
options.feedback: That is a time on its own. The rate is the change divided by that time.

items.stem: A test tube is sealed with a bung. What can get in or out?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 — open and closed containers

options.text: nothing
options.feedback: Nothing at all. Section 4 calls that a closed system, and equilibrium needs one.

options.text: gases only
options.feedback: A bung stops the gas as well. That is the point of using one, and it is what makes the reverse reaction possible.

options.text: heat only
options.feedback: Heat can still pass through the glass, but no substance can. Closed is about substances.

items.stem: What does a reversible reaction mean?

options.text: the products can react to form the reactants again
options.feedback: Both directions are real, which is why the equation carries a double arrow.

options.text: the reactants can be returned to their original state
options.feedback: 'Original state' is the phrasing Summer 2025 examiners refused. Name the substances: the products react to form the reactants again.

options.text: the reaction can be stopped at any point
options.feedback: Stopping a reaction is not reversing it. Reversible means the products turn back into the reactants.

options.text: the reaction gives out heat one way and takes it in the other
options.feedback: That is true of a reversible reaction, but it is not what the word means. The meaning is about direction, not energy.

items.stem: Blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate is heated. What is seen, and what is formed?

options.text: blue to white; anhydrous copper(II) sulfate and water
options.feedback: Heating drives the water out of the crystals and leaves the white anhydrous solid.

options.text: blue to black; copper(II) oxide and water
options.feedback: Copper(II) oxide is black, but it comes from heating the carbonate. Here the water simply leaves the crystals.

options.text: white to blue; hydrated copper(II) sulfate
options.feedback: That is the reverse change, the one you see when water is added. Heating goes blue to white.

options.text: blue to colourless; copper(II) sulfate solution
options.feedback: A solution is what you get by adding a lot of water. Heating leaves a dry white powder.

items.stem: A reaction in a sealed vessel has reached dynamic equilibrium. Which statement is true?

options.text: the forward and reverse reactions are going at the same rate
options.feedback: Equal rates. Both reactions are still running, which is what the word dynamic records.

options.text: the amounts of reactants and products are equal
options.feedback: The amounts stay constant, but there is no reason for them to be equal to each other. It is the rates that are equal.

options.text: both reactions have stopped
options.feedback: Nothing has stopped. It only looks still because each reaction undoes the other exactly.

options.text: the forward reaction has finished and the reverse one has started
options.feedback: They run at the same time, not one after the other. From the start both are happening.

items.stem: Why must the system be closed for a dynamic equilibrium to be reached?

options.text: so that no substance can escape and the reverse reaction can keep up
options.feedback: A product that has left the container cannot react back, so the two rates could never become equal.

options.text: so that the temperature cannot change
options.feedback: Closed is about substances, not heat. Heat still passes through the glass of a stoppered flask.

options.text: so that the reaction is safe
options.feedback: Safety may be a reason for using a bung, but it is not the reason the definition names.

options.text: so that the forward reaction stops
options.feedback: Neither reaction stops at equilibrium. Closing the system lets the reverse reaction catch up with the forward one.

items.stem: Which set of conditions can be altered to change the direction of a reversible reaction?

options.text: temperature, pressure and concentration
options.feedback: All three. Temperature is the one nearly everybody names; the marks are usually in the other two.

options.text: temperature only
options.feedback: Summer 2025 records exactly this: many named temperature and few mentioned concentration or pressure.

options.text: colour and mass
options.feedback: Colour is something you observe, and mass is conserved. Neither is a condition you set.

options.text: the size of the container only
options.feedback: Changing the container's size changes the pressure, so say pressure — and add temperature and concentration.

items.stem: On the rate-against-time graph for a reversible reaction in a sealed vessel, the two curves meet at 60 s. What is happening at 60 s?
items.skill: Read the equilibrium point from a graph

options.text: the forward and reverse rates have become equal
options.feedback: Both are 4 from then on, and the amounts stop changing.

options.text: the reaction has finished
options.feedback: Neither curve has fallen to zero, so both reactions are still going. They are simply going at the same rate.

options.text: the amounts of reactant and product have become equal
options.feedback: The graph plots rates, not amounts. Equal rates make the amounts constant, not equal.

options.text: the reverse reaction has overtaken the forward one
options.feedback: The curves meet and then run together; neither goes above the other.

parts.stem:
Blue crystals of hydrated copper(II) sulfate are heated in a test tube until the solid is white. The tube is allowed to cool and water is then added to the white solid.
Describe what happens at each stage, and explain how this demonstration shows that the reaction is reversible.
This question also assesses the quality of your written communication, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist chemical terms used widely and accurately; organised with clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar good enough that the meaning is clear throughout.
Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist chemical vocabulary; organised with some clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the intended meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: On heating, the blue crystals turn white.
Water is driven off and condenses at the cool end of the tube.
The white solid is anhydrous copper(II) sulfate.
When water is added the white solid turns blue again.
Heat is given out when the water is added, so the tube becomes hot.
The same reaction has been driven in both directions, so it is reversible.
It is written with the reversible sign rather than a single arrow.

scheme.for: a banded description of both stages and the conclusion: blue to white on heating, water driven off, the white solid named, white to blue on adding water, heat given out, and the deduction that the reaction is reversible and carries the reversible sign
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Two stages, and what you would see in each.
Finish with what the two stages together prove.
parts.workedSolution: On heating, the blue crystals of hydrated copper(II) sulfate turn white and droplets of water collect at the cool end of the tube, because the water bonded into the crystals is driven off. The white solid left is anhydrous copper(II) sulfate. When water is added to it, the solid turns blue again and the tube becomes hot, because heat is given out. The same reaction has been driven in one direction by heating and in the other by adding water, so it is reversible and is written with the reversible sign rather than a single arrow.

findTheMistake.stem:
Ruairí is asked: 'A reversible reaction in a sealed flask has reached a dynamic equilibrium. Finish this sentence in two ways, giving a statement that is true at that point each time: at equilibrium … [2]'
His answer:
studentWorking: … the amounts of the reactants and the products are equal,
… and the amounts of reactants and products remain constant.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The second line is exactly right. The first should be about the rates, not the amounts: at equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions are going at the same rate. The amounts stay constant, but there is no reason at all for them to be equal to each other.
correction: … the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal,
findTheMistake.feedback: One of the two marks. The amounts line stands; the rates line is the one to fix. Summer 2024 examiners saw the same swap again and again, with the concentration written where the rates belonged. Rates first, amounts second, every time.

findTheMistake.stem:
Aisling is asked: 'Carbon monoxide reacts with hydrogen to form methanol, CH₃OH, and the reaction goes both ways. Give its balanced symbol equation. [3]'
Her working:
studentWorking: Balance the hydrogen: CH₃OH holds 4 H atoms, so 2H₂
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Her formulae and her balancing are right. The question says the reaction is reversible, and a single arrow claims it goes one way only: the reversible sign is a mark of its own, and she has lost it.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two of the three marks: the formulae and the balancing stand. Whenever a question says reversible or equilibrium, write ⇌. The Summer 2024 report names the missing equilibrium sign as a common error.

prompts.answer: So nothing escapes and the reverse reaction can keep pace.
